about: Materials (CIVE40007) is a 5-credit core module in the first year of Imperial's MEng Civil Engineering, running across the Autumn and Spring terms (2026–27 programme specification). No public module descriptor or topic list could be accessed (the department's syllabus page links to a module summary that could not be opened), so the topics in this pack are a standard first-year civil engineering materials course built from the module title and description (properties and testing, steel, concrete, timber, durability, and time-dependent and composite behaviour), not the department's confirmed syllabus. We could not find module-level assessment details; the programme specification gives only the Year 1 split as a whole (32% coursework, 68% examination). Check the module's own handbook or course pages for the exact content.
topics: Mechanical properties and testing of construction materials
Thermal and time-dependent behaviour; steel and concrete working together

notes.h: Mechanical properties, testing and characteristic strength
notes.body:
Civil engineers specify materials by a small number of properties measured in standard tests. Understanding what each property means, how it is measured and how test results become design values is the starting point for steel, concrete and timber alike.

Key properties
- Stress σ = F/A and strain ε = ΔL/L. In the elastic range σ = Eε, where E is Young's modulus.
- Strength: the stress at yield (for steel) or at failure (for concrete in compression, timber in bending).
- Stiffness: E controls deflections and buckling. Approximate values: structural steel 210 GPa (the value used in Eurocode 3), concrete about 30–35 GPa for common strength classes (Eurocode 2 gives a mean modulus Ecm of about 33 GPa for C30/37), softwood timber along the grain around 7–12 GPa.
- Ductility: the plastic strain a material can sustain before fracture. Ductile materials (steel) give warning and redistribute load; brittle ones (plain concrete in tension, glass) do not.
- Toughness: resistance to crack growth or the energy absorbed in fracture; for steel it is measured with the Charpy impact test.
- Hardness and fatigue resistance matter for wearing surfaces and for cyclically loaded structures such as bridges.

Standard tests (examples)
- Tensile test of metals (BS EN ISO 6892-1): gives E, yield or 0.2% proof strength, tensile strength and elongation.
- Compressive strength of concrete cubes or cylinders (BS EN 12390-3), usually at 28 days.
- Bending tests on timber, and slump tests for fresh concrete workability.

Worked example: a 20 mm diameter steel bar carries 100 kN. A = π × 20²/4 = 314 mm², so σ = 100,000/314 = 318 MPa. With E = 210 GPa the strain is 1.52 × 10⁻³ and a 3 m bar extends by about 4.5 mm.

Variability and characteristic strength
Materials vary: no two concrete cubes give the same result. Design therefore uses a characteristic strength, defined as the value below which only 5% of results are expected to fall. If results are normally distributed with mean fm and standard deviation s:
- fk = fm − 1.64s.
- Example: six cubes give 41.5, 44.0, 46.5, 39.0, 47.5 and 43.0 MPa. Mean = 43.6 MPa, sample standard deviation = 3.15 MPa, so fk ≈ 43.6 − 1.64 × 3.15 ≈ 38.4 MPa.
- In practice small samples need statistical care, and conformity rules for concrete are set out in the concrete standards; the principle is the same.

From characteristic to design values
Eurocodes divide characteristic strengths by partial factors for materials: for example γc = 1.5 for concrete and γs = 1.15 for reinforcement in Eurocode 2 (the recommended values, adopted in the UK National Annex), and γM0 = 1.0 for steel cross-sections in Eurocode 3. The more variable or brittle the material, the larger the factor. (Loads have their own partial factors.)

Exam tips: always show the area calculation with units, distinguish mean from characteristic values, and explain why brittle materials need larger safety margins.

Steel is the civil engineer's ductile, strong and reliable material, used for frames, bridges and as reinforcement in concrete. Its behaviour follows from its composition, microstructure and processing.

What steel is
- Steel is iron with a small amount of carbon, plus elements such as manganese. Structural steels have low carbon contents (about 0.2% or less), giving a microstructure mainly of ferrite with some pearlite.
- More carbon raises strength and hardness but reduces ductility, toughness and weldability. Structural steels balance these properties.
- Strength also comes from fine grain size, alloying and controlled rolling; quenching and tempering is used for higher-strength grades.

Stress–strain behaviour
- Linear elastic up to a distinct yield point (for hot-rolled mild steels), then a yield plateau, then strain hardening up to the ultimate tensile strength, then necking and fracture.
- Approximate properties: E = 210 GPa, ν = 0.3, density about 7850 kg/m³, coefficient of thermal expansion about 12 × 10⁻⁶ per °C.
- Steel behaves similarly in tension and compression (although slender members buckle).

Grades (BS EN 10025)
- Designations such as S275 and S355: "S" means structural, and the number is the minimum yield strength in MPa for the thinnest products (up to 16 mm). Yield strength reduces slightly for thicker plates.
- Sub-grades such as JR, J0 and J2 specify the Charpy impact energy (27 J) at +20 °C, 0 °C and −20 °C respectively: a measure of toughness, important to avoid brittle fracture in cold conditions and thick sections.

Ductile-to-brittle transition
Ferritic steels become brittle below a transition temperature. Low temperature, thick sections, high loading rates and notches (including weld defects) all promote brittle fracture, which is why toughness sub-grades are chosen according to service temperature and thickness.

Reinforcing steel
- In the UK, reinforcement to BS 4449 is grade B500 with characteristic yield strength fyk = 500 MPa, in ductility classes A, B and C (C most ductile).
- Bars are ribbed to give mechanical bond with concrete, so that the two materials strain together.
- Eurocode 2 uses Es = 200 GPa for reinforcement.

Connections and fabrication
Steel is joined by bolting and welding. Welding brings local heating that can alter the microstructure in the heat-affected zone and leave residual stresses; correct procedures and weldable grades are essential.

Behaviour in fire
Steel loses strength and stiffness as it heats. In Eurocode 3's fire rules (EN 1993-1-2), the reduction factor for the effective yield strength of carbon steel at 600 °C is 0.47, so roughly half the ambient yield strength remains. Thin unprotected members heat quickly, so fire protection (boards, sprays, intumescent paint) is often required.

Exam tips: be able to explain what each part of a grade name means, describe the stress–strain curve with labelled features, and link carbon content to the strength–ductility trade-off.

notes.h: Cement and concrete: making, hydration and strength
notes.body:
Concrete is the most widely used construction material. It is cheap, mouldable and strong in compression, but weak in tension and dependent on how it is mixed, placed and cured.

Portland cement
- Made by heating limestone and clay (or shale) to about 1450 °C in a kiln to form clinker, which is ground with a little gypsum.
- Clinker contains four main compounds, written in cement chemists' notation (C = CaO, S = SiO₂, A = Al₂O₃, F = Fe₂O₃): C3S (alite), C2S (belite), C3A and C4AF. C3S gives most early strength; C2S contributes later strength; C3A reacts very fast, and gypsum is added to control it and prevent a flash set.
- Manufacturing cement releases a lot of CO₂ (from fuel and from decomposing limestone), so replacing part of it with supplementary materials such as ground granulated blast-furnace slag (GGBS) or fly ash is common.

Hydration
- Cement reacts with water (hydration), releasing heat, to form calcium silicate hydrate (C-S-H), the glue that gives strength, and calcium hydroxide (CH), which keeps the pore water strongly alkaline.
- Strength grows rapidly in the first days and continues to rise slowly for months while water is available. Hence curing: keeping concrete moist (and not too cold) after placing.
- Large pours generate heat; temperature differences can cause early-age thermal cracking.

Water–cement ratio
- The water/cement ratio (w/c) is the mass of free water divided by the mass of cement. 175 kg of water with 350 kg of cement gives w/c = 0.5.
- Abrams' law: for fully compacted concrete, strength falls as w/c rises. Extra water leaves pores when it evaporates, raising porosity and permeability, reducing both strength and durability.
- Only a fraction of the water is needed chemically; the rest is for workability. Plasticisers and superplasticisers allow low w/c with good workability.

Constituents and fresh properties
- Aggregates (sand and gravel or crushed rock) make up most of the volume, giving bulk, stiffness and dimensional stability.
- Workability is commonly checked with the slump test.
- Concrete must be compacted (vibrated) to remove trapped air voids.

Hardened properties (approximate)
- Strength classes are written C30/37: characteristic cylinder strength 30 MPa / characteristic cube strength 37 MPa.
- Tensile strength is roughly a tenth of compressive strength; Eurocode 2 (EN 1992-1-1, Table 3.1) gives a mean tensile strength of about 2.9 MPa and a mean modulus of about 33 GPa for C30/37.
- Density is about 2400 kg/m³ (plain concrete).
- Because it cracks at low tensile stress, concrete is reinforced with steel bars placed where tension occurs, or prestressed.

Exam tips: define w/c precisely (free water over cement, by mass), link it to porosity, strength and durability in one chain, and decode strength-class notation correctly.

Timber is a natural composite of cellulose fibres in a lignin matrix, grown rather than manufactured. It is light, renewable and easy to work, but anisotropic, variable and sensitive to moisture. Understanding why is the key to using it well.

Structure
- Trees are softwoods (conifers, e.g. spruce, pine, fir) or hardwoods (broadleaved trees, e.g. oak, beech). The terms are botanical: balsa is a hardwood.
- Wood consists mainly of long hollow cells aligned with the trunk. This grain direction gives very different properties along and across the grain.
- Growth rings, knots (where branches grew), slope of grain and splits are natural features that reduce strength.

Anisotropy
- Along the grain, timber is stiff and strong for its weight; across the grain, stiffness and strength are many times lower (often by an order of magnitude or more).
- Tension perpendicular to the grain is especially weak, so connections and curved members must avoid it.
- Typical approximate values for C24 softwood in BS EN 338: characteristic bending strength 24 MPa, mean modulus parallel to the grain 11 GPa, mean density about 420 kg/m³.

Moisture
- Moisture content (MC) is the mass of water divided by the oven-dry mass of wood. A piece weighing 25 kg wet and 20 kg oven-dry has MC = 5/20 = 25%.
- Below the fibre saturation point (roughly 25–30% MC), water held in the cell walls affects strength and stiffness: drier timber is stronger and stiffer, and it shrinks as it dries, much more across the grain than along it.
- Timber in service settles to an equilibrium moisture content set by the surrounding humidity. Eurocode 5 uses service classes 1–3 and modification factors (kmod, kdef) to allow for moisture and load duration.
- Persistently high moisture (above about 20%) allows fungal decay.

Grading and strength classes
- Each piece is graded visually or by machine, then assigned to a strength class in BS EN 338: C classes for softwoods (e.g. C16, C24) and D classes for hardwoods (e.g. D30). The number is the characteristic bending strength in MPa.

Time-dependent behaviour
- Timber creeps under sustained load, more so at higher moisture content, so long-term deflection exceeds the initial value.
- Strength depends on load duration: timber can carry higher stresses briefly than permanently.

Engineered wood
- Glued laminated timber (glulam): layers glued with grain parallel, allowing long, curved and large members and dispersing defects.
- Cross-laminated timber (CLT): layers glued at right angles, making stiff panels for walls and floors.
- Laminated veneer lumber (LVL), plywood and OSB: thin veneers or strands bonded together, giving more uniform properties.

Fire: timber burns, but large sections char on the outside; the char layer insulates the core, which keeps much of its strength, so massive timber can achieve useful fire resistance when designed for charring.

Exam tips: define moisture content on the oven-dry basis, explain anisotropy from cell structure, and remember that the number in a strength class is the characteristic bending strength.

notes.h: Durability: corrosion of steel, deterioration of concrete and decay of timber
notes.body:
Most structures are designed to last 50 years or more. Many fail to do so not through overload but through slow deterioration. Durability depends on the material, the environment and the detailing.

Corrosion of steel
- Corrosion is electrochemical. At anodic sites iron dissolves: Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻. At cathodic sites, oxygen and water consume the electrons: O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻. The products combine and oxidise further to form rust.
- It needs both water and oxygen, and an electrolyte path; salts accelerate it by increasing conductivity and breaking down protective films.
- Rust occupies several times the volume of the steel it replaces, which is why corroding reinforcement cracks and spalls the concrete cover.
- Protection for structural steel: paint systems; hot-dip galvanising, in which zinc both seals the surface and acts as a sacrificial anode at scratches because it is more reactive than iron; weathering steel, which forms an adherent protective patina in suitable climates; and cathodic protection.
- Contact between dissimilar metals in an electrolyte causes galvanic corrosion of the more reactive one.

Why steel in concrete is normally protected
- The pore solution of concrete is highly alkaline (pH around 12.5–13.5) because of calcium hydroxide. At this pH a thin passive oxide film forms on steel and corrosion is negligible.
- Two main processes destroy this protection:
 - Carbonation: CO₂ from the air diffuses in and reacts with calcium hydroxide, CO₂ + Ca(OH)₂ → CaCO₃ + H₂O, lowering the pH below about 9. When the carbonation front reaches the steel, the passive film is lost. Its depth grows roughly as x = k√t. With k = 4 mm/√year and cover 30 mm, the front reaches the steel after about (30/4)² ≈ 56 years.
 - Chlorides from de-icing salts or seawater break down the passive film locally even at high pH, causing pitting corrosion, which can be severe.
- Defences: adequate cover, low w/c ratio, good compaction and curing, supplementary cementitious materials (GGBS, fly ash) that reduce chloride penetration, crack-width control, and in severe cases coatings, stainless or coated bars, or cathodic protection.
- BS EN 206 groups environments into exposure classes, e.g. XC (carbonation), XD (chlorides other than seawater), XS (seawater) and XF (freeze–thaw), which set limits on the mix; minimum cover for each exposure class then comes from Eurocode 2 with its UK National Annex and BS 8500.

Other concrete deterioration
- Freeze–thaw: water expands about 9% on freezing in saturated pores; air entrainment provides tiny voids that relieve the pressure.
- Sulfate attack: sulfates in soil or groundwater react with cement hydrates to form expansive products.
- Alkali–silica reaction (ASR): reactive silica in some aggregates reacts with alkalis in the pore solution, forming a gel that swells and cracks the concrete.

Timber
- Fungal decay needs moisture content above about 20%, oxygen and suitable temperatures. Keep timber dry by detailing (ventilation, drainage, avoiding ground contact) and use durable species or preservative treatment where wetting is unavoidable.
- Some insects attack timber, particularly sapwood.

Exam tips: write the anode and cathode reactions, explain passivation and its two enemies (carbonation and chlorides), and use x = k√t with consistent units.

notes.h: Thermal movement, creep and shrinkage, and how steel and concrete share load
notes.body:
Structures move and deform even when loads do not change: temperature changes, drying and sustained load all cause strains. When these movements are restrained, stresses arise; when materials are combined, load is shared according to stiffness.

Thermal strain
- Free thermal strain ε = αΔT, where α is the coefficient of thermal expansion. Approximate values: steel about 12 × 10⁻⁶ per °C, concrete about 10 × 10⁻⁶ per °C (depending on aggregate), timber along the grain a few × 10⁻⁶ per °C.
- If the movement is fully restrained, the stress is σ = EαΔT. A steel member fully restrained over a 30 °C rise: 210,000 × 12 × 10⁻⁶ × 30 = 75.6 MPa in compression, a large stress produced without any load.
- Expansion joints, bearings and sliding connections allow movement in long structures such as bridges and rails.
- Steel and concrete have similar α, which is one of the reasons reinforced concrete works: temperature changes do not break the bond between them.

Shrinkage of concrete
- Drying shrinkage: as water leaves the pores, the paste contracts. Long-term shrinkage strains of a few hundred microstrain are typical. Autogenous shrinkage occurs as hydration consumes water, important in low-w/c concrete.
- Restrained shrinkage causes cracking, controlled by reinforcement, joints and curing.

Creep
- Creep is strain that increases with time under sustained stress. In concrete, long-term creep strain can be one to three times the initial elastic strain, depending on the age at loading, humidity, member size and mix.
- The creep coefficient φ is defined so that total strain = elastic strain × (1 + φ). A simple approach uses an effective modulus Ec,eff = Ec/(1 + φ). With Ec = 33 GPa and φ = 2, Ec,eff = 11 GPa.
- Creep increases long-term deflections and causes loss of prestress, but it also relieves stresses from restrained movements.
- Timber creeps too, especially when damp (Eurocode 5 uses kdef); steel creeps significantly only at high temperatures.

Composite action: the reinforced concrete column
If steel and concrete are bonded, they have the same strain (compatibility). The axial force is shared in proportion to their axial stiffnesses:
- N = σcAc + σsAs with σc = Ecε and σs = Esε, so ε = N/(EcAc + EsAs).
- The modular ratio n = Es/Ec lets the steel be replaced by an equivalent concrete area nAs (a transformed section).

Worked example: a 300 × 300 mm column with four 20 mm bars (As = 1257 mm², Ac = 88,743 mm²), Ec = 30 GPa, Es = 200 GPa, N = 2000 kN.
- ε = 2 × 10⁶/(30,000 × 88,743 + 200,000 × 1257) = 6.86 × 10⁻⁴.
- σc = 20.6 MPa and σs = 137 MPa; the steel, only 1.4% of the area, carries about 8.6% of the load.
- Under sustained load, creep (say φ = 2, Ec,eff = 10 GPa) raises the strain to about 1.76 × 10⁻³: the steel stress rises to about 351 MPa and its share to about 22%, while the concrete stress falls to about 17.6 MPa. Creep transfers load from concrete to steel.

Exam tips: state the compatibility assumption explicitly, keep units consistent (N and mm² give MPa), and remember that a restrained thermal stress is independent of the member's length.

questions.q: Concrete cubes have mean strength 45 MPa and standard deviation 4 MPa. Assuming a normal distribution, what is the characteristic strength?
questions.why: fk = fm − 1.64s = 45 − 1.64 × 4 = 38.4 MPa, the 5% lower fractile. 51.6 MPa adds the margin instead of subtracting it, giving the 95% upper value. 37.0 MPa uses 2s rather than 1.64s, a different (about 2.3%) fractile. 45.0 MPa is the mean, which half of the results fall below.

questions.q: A 20 mm diameter steel bar, 3 m long (E = 210 GPa), carries an axial tension of 100 kN. What is its elastic extension?
questions.why: A = π × 20²/4 = 314 mm², σ = 318 MPa, ε = 318/210,000 = 1.52 × 10⁻³, and ΔL = 1.52 × 10⁻³ × 3000 = 4.5 mm. 1.1 mm comes from using A = πd² (treating the diameter as the radius), which makes the stress four times too small. 3.6 mm comes from using A = d² = 400 mm², as if the bar were square. 0.0045 mm comes from multiplying the strain by the length in metres (3) and labelling the answer in millimetres.

questions.q: Six concrete cubes give 41.5, 44.0, 46.5, 39.0, 47.5 and 43.0 MPa. Calculate the mean, standard deviation and characteristic strength, and explain why design uses the characteristic rather than the mean value.
markScheme: Sample standard deviation ≈ 3.15 MPa
Design uses fk because only about 5% of the material should be weaker; using the mean would mean half the concrete is weaker than assumed
questions.modelAnswer: Mean = (41.5 + 44.0 + 46.5 + 39.0 + 47.5 + 43.0)/6 = 261.5/6 = 43.6 MPa. Squared deviations sum to about 49.7, so s = √(49.7/5) ≈ 3.15 MPa. fk = 43.6 − 1.64 × 3.15 ≈ 38.4 MPa. Strength varies from batch to batch; using the mean would mean that half the concrete placed is weaker than the design assumes. The characteristic value is exceeded by 95% of the material, and partial factors then add a further margin for remaining uncertainties.

questions.q: In the steel designation S355J2, what does 355 indicate?
options: Minimum yield strength of 355 MPa for thin sections
questions.why: The number in an S-designation is the minimum yield strength in MPa for nominal thicknesses up to 16 mm. Reading it as the ultimate tensile strength confuses yield with ultimate; the ultimate strength is considerably higher. Reading it as carbon content mixes it up with chemical designation systems, and structural steels contain only about 0.2% carbon. The impact requirement is given by the J2 suffix (27 J at −20 °C), not by the number.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of the ribs on reinforcing bars?
options: To improve bond with the surrounding concrete
To raise the bar's tensile strength
To reduce corrosion of the bar
To reduce the weight of the bar
questions.why: The ribs interlock mechanically with the concrete so forces transfer between the two materials and they deform together. They do not raise tensile strength, which comes from the steel's composition and processing; this confuses surface shape with material strengthening. They do nothing to stop corrosion, which is prevented by the alkaline concrete cover. Weight per metre is set by the bar's nominal size, so the ribs are not there to save weight.

questions.q: A 20 mm diameter S355 steel tie carries 100 kN. Check whether it yields (take γM0 = 1.0) and describe, with a sketch in words, the stress–strain curve you would expect if the tie were tested to failure.
markScheme: A = 314 mm², σ = 318 MPa
318 MPa < 355 MPa, so no yield; utilisation ≈ 0.90
Linear elastic region with slope E = 210 GPa up to a distinct upper/lower yield point
Yield plateau followed by strain hardening up to the ultimate tensile strength
Necking then ductile fracture at large strain
questions.modelAnswer: A = π × 20²/4 = 314 mm² and σ = 100,000/314 = 318 MPa. The design yield strength is 355/1.0 = 355 MPa, so the tie does not yield; utilisation = 318/355 ≈ 0.90. In a tensile test a hot-rolled S355 bar would show a straight elastic line with slope 210 GPa, a distinct yield point near 355 MPa (or above), a yield plateau where strain increases at roughly constant stress, then strain hardening up to the ultimate tensile strength. After that the bar necks, the load falls, and it fractures in a ductile way at a large total elongation.

questions.q: A concrete mix contains 350 kg of cement and 175 kg of free water per cubic metre. What is its water/cement ratio?
questions.why: w/c = 175/350 = 0.50. 2.00 is the cement/water ratio, i.e. the fraction inverted. 0.33 is water divided by the total of water and cement (175/525). 0.175 divides the water content by 1000 kg rather than by the cement content.

questions.q: What does the concrete strength class C30/37 mean?
options: Characteristic cylinder strength 30 MPa and characteristic cube strength 37 MPa
Characteristic cube strength 30 MPa and characteristic cylinder strength 37 MPa
Mean cylinder strength 30 MPa and mean cube strength 37 MPa
Compressive strength between a minimum of 30 MPa and a maximum of 37 MPa
questions.why: The first number is the characteristic cylinder strength and the second the characteristic cube strength; cubes give higher values because of greater platen restraint. Putting 30 on the cube swaps the two specimens. Calling them mean strengths confuses characteristic (5% fractile) with mean values; the mean is higher. Reading the pair as a minimum and maximum misinterprets the notation, which gives the same characteristic strength measured on two specimen shapes.

questions.q: Explain how the water/cement ratio affects the strength and durability of hardened concrete, and how a low w/c can still be workable.
markScheme: w/c = mass of free water/mass of cement
Water not used in hydration leaves capillary pores
Higher w/c means higher porosity, so lower strength (Abrams' law)
Higher porosity and permeability let CO₂, chlorides and water in, reducing durability
Plasticisers/superplasticisers give workability at low w/c
questions.modelAnswer: The water/cement ratio is the mass of free water divided by the mass of cement. Hydration consumes only part of the water; the rest stays in capillary pores that are left empty when it dries. So the higher the w/c, the more porous the hardened paste. Porosity reduces strength (Abrams' law: strength falls as w/c rises) and, because the pores connect, increases permeability, which lets water, carbon dioxide and chlorides penetrate and leads to reinforcement corrosion and freeze–thaw damage. A low w/c on its own makes a stiff mix that is hard to place, so plasticisers or superplasticisers are added to disperse the cement particles and restore workability without extra water.

questions.q: A timber sample weighs 25.0 kg when wet and 20.0 kg after oven-drying. What is its moisture content?
questions.why: MC = (25 − 20)/20 = 25%, using the oven-dry mass as the base. 20% divides the water by the wet mass (5/25), the wet-basis definition, which is not the convention for timber. 80% is the dry mass as a fraction of the wet mass (20/25). 5% reports the 5 kg of water as if it were a percentage.

questions.q: What does the strength class C24 in BS EN 338 indicate?
options: A softwood with characteristic bending strength 24 MPa
A softwood with mean modulus of elasticity 24 GPa
A softwood with mean bending strength 24 MPa
A softwood with characteristic compressive strength 24 MPa along the grain
questions.why: The C stands for coniferous (softwood) and the number is the characteristic (5% fractile) bending strength in MPa. Reading it as a modulus of 24 GPa confuses strength with stiffness; C24's mean modulus is about 11 GPa. Reading it as a mean strength confuses the characteristic value with the mean, which is higher. Reading it as compressive strength picks the wrong property: the class is defined by bending strength.

questions.q: Explain why the mechanical properties of timber depend on (a) the direction of loading relative to the grain and (b) moisture content, and state one design consequence of each.
markScheme: (a) Wood is made of long cells aligned with the trunk, like a fibre composite
(a) Stiff and strong along the grain; much weaker across it, especially in tension perpendicular to grain
(a) Consequence: orient members along the grain and avoid tension perpendicular to grain at connections and in curved members
(b) Below fibre saturation, water in cell walls reduces strength and stiffness; drying causes shrinkage mainly across the grain
(b) Consequence: design for service class (kmod, kdef), allow for shrinkage movement, keep MC below about 20% to prevent decay
questions.modelAnswer: (a) Timber consists mainly of long hollow cells aligned with the trunk, with cellulose fibres in their walls, so it behaves like an aligned fibre composite. Loaded along the grain, the stiff fibres carry the load; across the grain, the cells crush or separate, so stiffness and strength are many times lower, and tension perpendicular to the grain is particularly weak. So members are oriented with the grain along the main stresses, and connections and curved members are detailed to avoid tension across the grain. (b) Below the fibre saturation point (roughly 25–30% moisture content), water held in the cell walls softens them: wetter timber is weaker, less stiff and creeps more, and drying makes it shrink, much more across the grain than along it. Designers therefore use the Eurocode 5 service class and kmod/kdef factors, allow for shrinkage movements at connections, and detail the building to keep moisture content below about 20% to prevent fungal decay.

questions.q: Carbonation depth in a concrete grows as x = k√t with k = 4 mm/√year. How long until it reaches reinforcement with 30 mm cover?
questions.why: t = (x/k)² = (30/4)² = 56.25 years. 7.5 years is x/k without squaring, treating depth as proportional to time. 120 years multiplies cover by k instead of dividing. 900 years squares the cover (30²) but forgets to divide by k².

questions.q: Why does hot-dip galvanised steel remain protected at a small scratch that exposes the steel?
options: Zinc is more reactive than iron, so it corrodes preferentially as a sacrificial anode
Zinc is more noble than iron, so it makes the steel the anode
The zinc layer raises the pH of moisture to the level found in concrete
Zinc acts only as a barrier, so a scratch is fully protected by the surrounding coating
questions.why: Zinc is more active than iron, so where both are exposed in moisture the zinc becomes the anode and corrodes instead, protecting the steel (sacrificial or cathodic protection). Calling zinc more noble reverses the galvanic series; a more noble coating, such as copper, would make exposed steel corrode faster. Galvanising does not work by creating concrete-like alkalinity; passivation by high pH is the mechanism for steel in concrete. A pure barrier coating would not protect bare steel at a scratch, which is precisely why the sacrificial action matters.

questions.q: Explain why reinforcing steel in good-quality concrete normally does not corrode, describe two processes that can start corrosion, and give three design measures that improve durability.
markScheme: High alkalinity (pH around 12.5–13.5) from Ca(OH)₂ forms a passive film on the steel
Carbonation: CO₂ reacts with Ca(OH)₂, pH falls below about 9, passivity lost when front reaches steel
Chlorides (de-icing salt, seawater) break down the film locally, causing pitting
Measures: adequate cover, low w/c and good compaction/curing, SCMs such as GGBS, crack control, coatings/stainless steel/cathodic protection in severe exposure
Rust expansion cracks and spalls cover once corrosion starts
questions.modelAnswer: The pore solution of concrete contains calcium hydroxide and is highly alkaline (pH around 12.5–13.5). In these conditions a thin, stable oxide film forms on the steel and corrosion is negligible. Carbonation destroys this: carbon dioxide diffuses in and converts calcium hydroxide to calcium carbonate, lowering the pH below about 9; once the carbonation front reaches the bars, the film is lost and corrosion can proceed where water and oxygen are present. Chlorides from de-icing salts or seawater break down the passive film locally even at high pH, causing pitting corrosion. As rust forms it expands, cracking and spalling the cover. Durability is improved by specifying adequate cover for the exposure class, using a low water/cement ratio with good compaction and curing to reduce permeability, using GGBS or fly ash to slow chloride ingress, controlling crack widths, and in severe exposures using coatings, stainless steel reinforcement or cathodic protection.

questions.q: A steel rail (E = 210 GPa, α = 12 × 10⁻⁶ per °C) is fully restrained and its temperature rises by 30 °C. What stress develops?
questions.why: σ = EαΔT = 210,000 MPa × 12 × 10⁻⁶ × 30 = 75.6 MPa, compressive because expansion is prevented. 2.52 MPa is Eα without multiplying by the temperature change. 3.6 × 10⁻⁴ is the free thermal strain αΔT, reported as if it were a stress. 75.6 kPa comes from taking E as 210 MPa instead of 210 GPa.

questions.q: A 300 × 300 mm column has four 20 mm bars (As = 1257 mm²). Ec = 30 GPa, Es = 200 GPa, axial load 2000 kN, perfect bond. What is the stress in the steel?
questions.why: ε = N/(EcAc + EsAs) = 2 × 10⁶/(30,000 × 88,743 + 200,000 × 1257) = 6.86 × 10⁻⁴, so σs = 200,000 × 6.86 × 10⁻⁴ = 137 MPa. 22.2 MPa is the load divided by the gross area (2 × 10⁶/90,000), which ignores the different stiffness of the steel. 20.6 MPa is the concrete stress, not the steel stress. 148 MPa multiplies that gross-area stress by the modular ratio (6.67 × 22.2) without using the transformed section, so it overestimates the steel stress.

questions.q: For the column above, the load is sustained and the concrete's creep coefficient is φ = 2. Using an effective modulus, find the new steel and concrete stresses and the share of load carried by the steel, and explain the result.
markScheme: σs ≈ 351 MPa, σc ≈ 17.6 MPa
Steel share rises from about 8.6% to about 22% of the load
Creep reduces concrete's effective stiffness; compatibility forces the steel to take more load (still below fyk = 500 MPa for B500)
questions.modelAnswer: Ec,eff = Ec/(1 + φ) = 30/3 = 10 GPa. ε = 2 × 10⁶/(10,000 × 88,743 + 200,000 × 1257) = 2 × 10⁶/(8.87 × 10⁸ + 2.51 × 10⁸) ≈ 1.76 × 10⁻³. Steel stress = 200,000 × 1.76 × 10⁻³ ≈ 351 MPa; concrete stress = 10,000 × 1.76 × 10⁻³ ≈ 17.6 MPa. Steel force = 351 × 1257 ≈ 441 kN, about 22% of the load, compared with about 8.6% initially. Under sustained load the concrete creeps, behaving as if less stiff; because bonded steel and concrete must share the same strain, load transfers from concrete to steel. The steel stress remains below the 500 MPa characteristic yield of B500 bars, but this effect must be considered in design.

questions.q:
A short reinforced concrete column, 300 mm × 300 mm, contains four 20 mm diameter B500 bars. Six cubes from its concrete gave 41.5, 44.0, 46.5, 39.0, 47.5 and 43.0 MPa at 28 days.
(a) Calculate the mean, standard deviation and characteristic cube strength of the concrete, and explain the meaning of the characteristic value. [5]
(b) Taking Ec = 30 GPa and Es = 200 GPa, find the stresses in the concrete and steel, and the proportion of load carried by the steel, when the column carries a short-term axial load of 2000 kN. [6]
(c) The load is sustained. Taking a creep coefficient of 2, estimate the long-term stresses and comment. [5]
(d) Explain why steel and concrete work well together in this column, referring to bond and thermal expansion. [4]
markScheme: (a) Characteristic = 5% fractile: 95% of results expected to exceed it
(b) As = 1257 mm², Ac = 88,743 mm²; ε = N/(EcAc + EsAs) = 6.86 × 10⁻⁴
(b) σc ≈ 20.6 MPa, σs ≈ 137 MPa; steel carries ≈ 173 kN ≈ 8.6%
(c) Ec,eff = 10 GPa; ε ≈ 1.76 × 10⁻³; σc ≈ 17.6 MPa, σs ≈ 351 MPa; steel share ≈ 22%
(c) Creep transfers load to steel; steel still below fyk = 500 MPa; long-term shortening about 2.6 times the initial value
(d) Ribbed bars bond so strains are equal; similar thermal expansion (about 10–12 × 10⁻⁶ per °C) avoids bond stresses with temperature; alkaline concrete protects the steel
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Mean = 261.5/6 = 43.6 MPa. Deviations from the mean: −2.08, 0.42, 2.92, −4.58, 3.92, −0.58; squares sum to about 49.7, so s = √(49.7/5) ≈ 3.15 MPa. Characteristic cube strength fk = 43.6 − 1.64 × 3.15 ≈ 38.4 MPa. This is the value below which only 5% of results would be expected to fall if strengths are normally distributed; designing with it rather than the mean ensures that nearly all the concrete is at least as strong as assumed.

(b) As = 4 × π × 20²/4 = 1257 mm²; Ac = 90,000 − 1257 = 88,743 mm². Bonded materials share the same strain: ε = N/(EcAc + EsAs) = 2 × 10⁶/(30,000 × 88,743 + 200,000 × 1257) = 2 × 10⁶/(2.662 × 10⁹ + 0.251 × 10⁹) = 6.86 × 10⁻⁴. σc = 30,000 × 6.86 × 10⁻⁴ = 20.6 MPa; σs = 200,000 × 6.86 × 10⁻⁴ = 137 MPa. Steel force = 137 × 1257 ≈ 173 kN, about 8.6% of the load; the concrete carries about 1827 kN.

(c) Ec,eff = 30/(1 + 2) = 10 GPa. ε = 2 × 10⁶/(10,000 × 88,743 + 200,000 × 1257) ≈ 1.76 × 10⁻³. σc ≈ 17.6 MPa; σs ≈ 351 MPa; steel force ≈ 441 kN, about 22% of the load. The column shortens about 2.6 times as much as initially (on a 4 m column, from about 2.7 mm to about 7.0 mm). Creep makes the concrete effectively softer, so load migrates into the steel; the steel stress is still below the 500 MPa characteristic yield of B500, but the concrete stress falls. Ignoring creep would underestimate steel stresses and long-term shortening.

(d) Ribbed bars interlock with the hardened concrete, so the two materials strain together and forces transfer between them, which is the assumption used in (b) and (c). Their coefficients of thermal expansion are similar (steel about 12 × 10⁻⁶ per °C, concrete about 10 × 10⁻⁶ per °C), so temperature changes do not generate large stresses at the interface that would break the bond. Concrete also protects the steel: its alkaline pore solution keeps the bars passive, and the cover provides fire insulation. The steel in turn supplies tensile capacity and ductility that concrete lacks.

questions.q: Compare structural steel, reinforced concrete and timber as materials for the frame of a medium-rise building. Your answer should consider mechanical behaviour, durability, behaviour in fire and how each material's properties are specified and made reliable for design.
markScheme: Mechanical: steel strong, stiff, ductile, same in tension and compression; concrete strong in compression, weak in tension so reinforced; timber light with good strength-to-weight along grain but anisotropic and less stiff
Specification: steel grades (S275/S355, toughness sub-grades), concrete strength classes (C30/37) and w/c limits, timber strength classes (C24) by grading; characteristic values and partial factors

Durability: steel corrosion needing coatings/galvanising; concrete protected by alkalinity but vulnerable to carbonation and chlorides, controlled by cover and low w/c; timber decay above about 20% MC, controlled by detailing and treatment
Fire: steel loses strength (about half at 600 °C) and needs protection; concrete performs well with adequate cover; massive timber chars and protects its core
Time-dependent effects: concrete creep and shrinkage, timber creep and moisture movement, steel creep negligible at normal temperatures
Balanced conclusion linking choice to span, loads, exposure, construction speed and sustainability
questions.modelAnswer:
Mechanical behaviour. Structural steel is strong (S355 has a minimum yield strength of 355 MPa for thin sections), stiff (E = 210 GPa) and ductile, and behaves similarly in tension and compression, although slender members buckle. It suits long spans and lightweight frames. Concrete is strong in compression (e.g. C30/37) but its tensile strength is only about a tenth of that, so it cracks in tension; bonded steel reinforcement carries tensile forces, and because the two materials have similar thermal expansion they stay bonded. Timber has an excellent strength-to-weight ratio along the grain (C24 has a characteristic bending strength of 24 MPa and a mean E of about 11 GPa at roughly 420 kg/m³) but is anisotropic, weak in tension across the grain and much less stiff than steel, so serviceability (deflection, vibration) often governs. Engineered products such as glulam and CLT overcome size limits and reduce variability.

Specification and reliability. Each material is graded: steel by BS EN 10025 grade with Charpy sub-grades for toughness; concrete by strength class with limits on w/c ratio and cover for its exposure class; timber by visual or machine grading into BS EN 338 classes. Design uses characteristic values (5% fractiles) divided by partial factors, larger for more variable materials (e.g. 1.5 for concrete, 1.15 for reinforcement in Eurocode 2).

Durability. Bare steel corrodes electrochemically in the presence of water and oxygen and needs paint or galvanising, or must be kept dry. Reinforcement in concrete is protected by the alkaline pore solution, but carbonation and chlorides can destroy this passivity; adequate cover, low w/c and good curing are the main defences. Timber is durable if kept below about 20% moisture content, but decays if persistently wet; good detailing, durable species or treatment are needed.

Fire. Steel loses strength as it heats (at 600 °C about half its yield strength remains under Eurocode 3's fire rules), so frames usually need protection. Concrete is non-combustible and insulating; with adequate cover the reinforcement stays cool, although spalling can occur. Timber burns, but large sections char at a fairly predictable rate and the char protects the core, so mass timber can be designed for fire resistance.

Time-dependent effects. Concrete creeps and shrinks, increasing deflections and transferring load to the reinforcement; timber creeps more when damp and moves with moisture; steel is effectively free of creep at normal temperatures.

Conclusion. The choice depends on span, loading, exposure, programme and environmental priorities: steel for speed and long spans, reinforced concrete for robustness, fire resistance and mass, timber for low weight and renewable sourcing. Many buildings combine them, for example timber floors on a steel frame with a concrete core.
